entries.title: Introduce Co-Created.
entries.content: Co-Created Story Over a decade ago, our founder met a corporate executive on an airplane who was struggling with a big shipping container logistics problem. He was intrigued by the problem and knew of many other entrepreneurs in his network who would be eager to help solve it if they knew about the scale and weight of the opportunity. / Their encounter was a catalyst for us to create a bridge between the corporate and startup worlds— where entrepreneurs could bring an energetic, tactical startup approach to corporate problems. / Today, Co-Created expands on a long history of corporate partnerships and venture building. Our model and methodology brings together corporations seeking to innovate and experienced, nimble entrepreneurs hungry to find their next venture. We continue to evolve our approach and carry out our mission of co-creating with purpose. / 6

entries.title: 5-10 Min
entries.content: 5-10 Min / Rollercoaster Check-In Checking-in is a simple way for a team to start a meeting, workshop, or activity. This rollercoaster version is a way for us to uncover any fears, concerns, or needs. This is a method to explore the whole group’s feelings in a playful and visual way. / • Take a sticky note and put your name on it • Consider how you feel • Place it at a points on the rollercoaster to explain dominant feeling right now. / Then we all share as a group, saying our name and how we feel. 21 / 1. 👀 “Curious but unsure” “I’m looking around, not sure what to expect. Feels new.” 2. 😐 “A little bored…” “We’re not doing much yet, just listening. Not sure where this is going.” 3. 😅 “Nervous energy” “Am I the only one who doesn’t get this?” 4. 🙃 “Trying to fit in” “Who are my people here? Am I being weird?” 5. 🤩 “This is actually kinda cool” “Ooh, that thing we just did was fun.” 6. 😵 “Too much at once” “I’m overwhelmed. Can we slow down a sec?” 7. 🥱 “Tired but surviving” “I didn’t sleep well but I’m still here!” 8. 🏄 “Catching the wave” “Okay, now I get it. This feels fun.” 9. 🧠 “Whoa, I’m learning stuff” “This is making me think differently.” 10. 👻 “Where did the time go?” “Wait, we’ve already done so much?”

entries.title: WHAT DO WE WANT
entries.content: WHAT DO WE WANT PARENT APPROVAL / FUN WITH FRIENDS INDEPENDENCE / What do us teens want? We want to have fun with friends. We want independence. But to do this, we need parent approval.

entries.title: VOLUNTEERING
entries.content: VOLUNTEERING ACTUALLY Builds community Helps teens make new friends Boosts social skills / There are a lot of benefits to volunteering. It helps build community by creating connections between the volunteer and the person they are helping. It is also extremely social, with teens having the opportunity to hang out with a bunch of people who are united towards one cause. It also boosts skills, as it teaches teens initiative, responsibility, and how to effectively communicate with others.

entries.title: BUT NOT ENOUGH PEOPLE
entries.content: BUT NOT ENOUGH PEOPLE VOLUNTEER LONG ENOUGH TO EXPERIENCE THE BENEFITS!#!! / So then, what’s wrong with volunteering? Well, the problem isn’t volunteering itself. It’s that teens don’t volunteer for long enough to realize these benefits, and some don’t even volunteer at all.

entries.title: The 5 Why’s
entries.content: The 5 Why’s Active Listening De nes a problem, then asks the question What makes“why” ve times, good often using the active listening? resulting explanation as a starting point for creative problem solving. / When we re ect and discuss, we tend to focus on multiple individuals and questions at once, moving around our attention and focus. Meanwhile, when we listen to others, we tend to do so in a discussion-oriented way, thinking about “what will I say next”, rather than listening to the other with full presence and attention. / One powerful way to explore a question or a problem is to use active listening with focus on one person at a time. fi / fl / fi

The person in this role should keep in mind: allow the focus to be on you, and let your reflection flow naturally, being guided by the active listener. / The active listener: The active listener’s role is to listen will full presence and focus. To listen with the whole body, to be curious, observe, paraphrase what he/she hears and guide the subject with open questions. This person should keep in mind: ask open questions to support the subject’s reflection; do not offer advice; listen with the whole body. / The observer: The observer’s role is to observe the process without speaking. To make observations from an outside perspective, to see and hear things that the listener and subject may not. This person should keep in mind: stay silent throughout the process; observe and make notes about what you see and hear; after the subject finishes, share the observations with the others. fl

entries.title: Anatomy of An Interview
entries.content: Anatomy of An Interview / Percentage of Warmup Core Interview Wrap-up Talking Warmup- This is the beginning of the interview and serves as an opportunity to build rapport 80% and get the respondent comfortable speaking. / Core Interview- This is the majority of the interview, when the interviewer is asking questions and the respondent is expanding 50% upon their answers. / Wrap-up- This is the final few minutes of an interview, and gives you the opportunity to ask respondents about parting thoughts, provide 20% referrals to other people, etc… / 5 min. 25 min. / Elapsed Time

entries.title: Design Research: Who Should Be Talking, and When?
entries.content: Design Research: Who Should Be Talking, and When? / Percentage of Warmup Core Interview Wrap-up Talking Warmup- At the beginning of the interview, you will likely do most of the speaking to get Respondent 80% things going. / Core Interview- However, as the conversation progresses, you should be 50% doing a small percentage of the speaking. / Wrap-up- Generally the last few minutes are Interviewer a mutual back and forth conversation. 20% / 5 min. 25 min. / Elapsed Time

entries.title: Planning For The Interview: The Discussion Guide
entries.content: Planning For The Interview: The Discussion Guide / Discussion guides serve an important purpose in the design research process. / ● Align teams on what to explore LIVING ● Aid interviewers to keep convo on track DOCUMENT Discussion guides are a living document that evolve as the teams’ understanding about a topic grows. / Discussion guides are not a script to be followed verbatim. SCRIPT

entries.title: Discussion Guide Formats
entries.content: Discussion Guide Formats / Discussion guides come in many formats, including: / ● Word.doc ● Miro ● Handwritten notebooks ● More… / It is more important that a discussion guide is functional and is manageable for an interviewer.

entries.title: Anatomy of a discussion guide: Intro
entries.content: Anatomy of a discussion guide: Intro Purpose of the introduction is to create an inviting environment that makes respondents feel at ease. Percentage of Warmup Core Interview Wrap-up Talking We do this by hitting several key beats Respondent 80% ● Lead with pleasantries ○ Breaks the ice, gets people talking ● Provide info before eliciting info ○ When flow of information is two-way, people 50% are more willing to provide info ● Make them feel safe ○ Remove tensions/ nerves or apprehensions Interviewer they may be feeling 20% ○ If they grow uncomfortable, use this as a call-back 5 min. 25 min. / Elapsed Time

entries.title: Not a people problem,
entries.content: Not a people problem, but a poverty problem When owners come to surrender dogs, Lori Weise asks a simple question: / If you could, would you like to keep your animal? / 75% of people said yes. / Lori Weise, Founder & President Downtown Dog Rescue (LA) CO-CREATED BEST PRACTICES

entries.title: Not a people problem,
entries.content: Not a people problem, but a poverty problem When owners come to surrender dogs, Lori Weise asks a simple question: / If you could, would you like to keep your animal? / 75% of people said yes. / But they are battling with problems of not having enough money to feed their kids at the end of the month. / Lori Weise, Founder & President Downtown Dog Rescue (LA) CO-CREATED BEST PRACTICES / When owners come to surrender dogs, Lori Weise asks a simple question: If you could, would you like to keep your animal? 75% of people said yes. But they are battling with problems of not having enough money to feed their kids at the end of the month. Her intervention programme provides free services to spay/neuter dogs, vaccines and basic pet supplies. She also helps homeless owners get dog licenses, enabling families to keep their pets and never have to surrender them to begin with. Keeping dogs out of the shelter to start turned out to be cheaper than nding a new home for the animal. / fi

entries.title: Better framing
entries.content: Better framing Affordability challenge for Low Income Families / Better solution Help dogs stay with their first family Cost: 85 ➔ 60 dollars / It was the insight about these "low-income families" that made Lori believe that there must be a solution to "how dogs can stay with their families" by looking at the deposit problem. So Lori's organization provided $150 to the families and asked them to return the amount when they moved away – thus allowing the dog to stay with the family, which is the best solution for everyone involved. / Although some of the money did not come back, there was still a better impact per dollar than for the other activities they had. When she looked at it, it cost an average of $85 to find a home for a dog, which was reduced to $60 with deposit assistance, a significant improvement in the average expense. / If you're interested in the story, Lori has published a book about this problem (First Home, Forever Home), where she describes it in detail. / This is an extremely striking example of how much it can matter when we have the framing right or wrong. This is an industry that has had a wrong perception of pet owners and their behavior for a long time. / It illustrates that you can rethink an industry that is over 40 years old – without new technology, it's not about blockchain or adtech – it's something we could have solved 40 years ago if we had understood the nature of the problem. It's about understanding the problems correctly...

entries.content: Not a people problem, but a poverty problem When owners come to surrender dogs, Lori Weise asks a simple question: / If you could, would you like to keep your animal? / 75% of people said yes. / Lori Weise, Founder & President Downtown Dog Rescue LA CO CREATED BEST PRACTICES - / ( / )

entries.title: Not a people problem,
entries.content: Not a people problem, but a poverty problem When owners come to surrender dogs, Lori Weise asks a simple question: / If you could, would you like to keep your animal? / 75% of people said yes. / But they are battling with problems of not having enough money to feed their kids at the end of the month. Lori Weise, Founder & President Downtown Dog Rescue LA CO CREATED BEST PRACTICES / When owners come to surrender dogs, Lori Weise asks a simple question: If you could, would you like to keep your animal? 75% of people said yes. But they are battling with problems of not having enough money to feed their kids at the end of the month. Her intervention programme provides free services to spay/neuter dogs, vaccines and basic pet supplies. She also helps homeless owners get dog licenses, enabling families to keep their pets and never have to surrender them to begin with. Keeping dogs out of the shelter to start turned out to be cheaper than finding a new home for the animal. - / ( / )

entries.title: Better framing
entries.content: Better framing Affordability challenge for Low Income Families / Better solution Help dogs stay with their first family Cost: 85 ➔ 60 dollars / It was the insight about these "low-income families" that made Lori believe that there must be a solution to "how dogs can stay with their families" by looking at the deposit problem. So Lori's organization provided $150 to the families and asked them to return the amount when they moved away – thus allowing the dog to stay with the family, which is the best solution for everyone involved. / Although some of the money did not come back, there was still a better impact per dollar than for the other activities they had. When she looked at it, it cost an average of $85 to find a home for a dog, which was reduced to $60 with deposit assistance, a significant improvement in the average expense. / If you're interested in the story, Lori has published a book about this problem First Home, Forever Home), where she describes it in detail. / This is an extremely striking example of how much it can matter when we have the framing right or wrong. This is an industry that has had a wrong perception of pet owners and their behavior for a long time. / It illustrates that you can rethink an industry that is over 40 years old – without new technology, it's not about blockchain or adtech – it's something we could have solved 40 years ago if we had understood the nature of the problem. It's about understanding the problems correctly... (

entries.title: Not all questions
entries.content: Not all questions are equally good at surfacing new perspectives / ot a discussion, it's an instruction. / You might find this conversation to be strange. We are good at being analytical and solving problems, but reframing is unfamiliar. / It's about asking questions to understand the problem. / Here are some of the strategies to help with reframing:

entries.title: Reframing Checklist
entries.content: Reframing Checklist Frame the Problem. What is the problem? Who s Involved? / Look Outside the Frame What are we missing? / Rethink the Goal Is there a better goal to pursue? / Examine Bright Spots Are there positive exceptions? / Look in the Mirror What is my role in creating the problem? / Take their Perspective What problem are they trying to solve? / X / 1. The first thing you saw in the elevator problem was not just seeing the initial problem (first framing) - what problems are we not considering - go 5 whys deep - why is the elevator slow, is it about something other than speed? / 2. Clarify and challenge the goal - what does success look like here? If you have a Christmas gathering with your family and end up in a political conversation with your drunk uncle, is the goal to win the argument - or is it about creating a cozy atmosphere? / 3. Bright spots: part of the root cause analysis framework - even when the problem arises - there are sometimes instances where it doesn't happen or where something affects the problem - 1.14 personal problem: who walks the dog - what changed? / 4. Look in the mirror - how am I contributing to creating the problem, "my kids use iPads too much" I am obviously the victim - it's them over there who create the problem for us. Although it may be true, is it possible that I myself contribute to the problem? (the customer or you as the consultant) / 5. Ask - take their own perspective - ask what they are trying to solve. entries.title: WH AT D OE S T H E CUSTOME R SAY
entries.content: WH AT D OE S T H E CUSTOME R SAY / How do we learn more about potential customers? The best founders don t guess—they listen. Customer interviews are the fastest, cheapest way to discover real problems and unmet needs. Before building anything, great teams ask: What are people struggling with? What are they trying to get done? Where are they making tradeoffs? Talking to customers helps you spot patterns, test assumptions, and avoid building the wrong thing. From startups to big companies, discovery interviews are a core habit. / Today s Mission: interviewing other stakeholders in the School ecosystem / X / Slide 23 Customer Discovery / o Introduce the concept o Emphasize why we do customer discovery o Discuss empathy and provide real world examples • • • / : / ’ / ’

entries.title: Background
entries.content: Background For the Lean Product Plan ‘Ensemble’ / American households have never been more diverse. The traditional nuclear family - a household with a father who is the sole breadwinner, a stay-at-home mother, and two children - is BOARD 4 much less common. After event / Today, the typical American family is multilayered and re ects a myriad of new social and family structures: multi-generational households, cohabitating couples, single parents, same-sex parents, and more. Can the basic joint-account experience really hold up? / The time is ripe to reconsider how we de ne “family” and reimagine the American nuclear family structure and its relative nancial instability and complexity, given among other factors the concentration of wealth among the baby boomer population, the low savings rate among Millennials and Gen-X, and lower marriage rates. / Today’s clients expect digital experiences that adapt to their ever-changing needs. In this workshop we will explore and unpack the life stages and milestones that present opportunities to solve these client needs with dynamic digital solutions. / fi / fi / fl

entries.title: The problem:
entries.content: The problem: / Volunteering hasn’t really changed in 1000s of years. It’s time to catch up to 2023… / Is there a way to volunteer in 2023 that does good for our community and gives a pat on the back to the volunteers?

entries.title: Introducing ServicePlus
entries.content: Introducing ServicePlus

entries.title: ServicePlus is an app that is owned by
entries.content: ServicePlus is an app that is owned by WTF and allows for young people to volunteer for events or organizations (partnered with WTF) in exchange for more data, or tickets to WTF sponsored events.

entries.title: It works like this:
entries.content: It works like this: - After creating an account in our app, you get the option to choose different events or organizations to volunteer at. - You choose a time and a place to volunteer. - After your volunteering is complete, you receive points that adds up over time as you volunteer. - This can earn you rewards like data, concert tickets, and more. - You receive extra points on the app for bringing friends.

entries.title: How do we make money?:
entries.content: How do we make money?: We make money through partnerships and sponsorships. We also make money because this idea will increase WTF’s exposure and get more people to use the service. People will tell their friends about WTF’s cool opportunities. We could also have ads in the app.

entries.title: We will make an impact on the industry by
entries.content: We will make an impact on the industry by measuring the amount of hours volunteered through our app.

entries.title: We will get our first customers by:
entries.content: We will get our first customers by: / Advertising to WTF’s current network of young people about this amazing opportunity. Advertising to parents as well because they would want their children to be doing good for the community, so their going to incentivize their kids to engage in this opportunity.

entries.title: Our vision is to increase the incentive to
entries.content: Our vision is to increase the incentive to volunteer, by giving back to our community, and establishing WTF as a unique enabler of young people’s views.

entries.content: VOLUNTEERING ACTUALLY Builds community Helps teens make new friends Boosts social skills / There are a lot of benefits to volunteering. It helps build community by creating connections between the volunteer and the person they are helping. It is also extremely social, with teens having the opportunity to hang out with a bunch of people who are united towards one cause. It also boosts skills, as it teaches teens initiative, responsibility, and how to effectively communicate with others.

entries.title: GREENFORCE is a national partnership
entries.content: GREENFORCE is a national partnership program that prepares rising high school seniors for green jobs in heavy industry through real exposure, networking, & college/ career guidance. / — think of it as the JROTC for the climate workforce.

entries.title: ● Applications through school/community orgs
entries.content: ● Applications through school/community orgs ● Visit clean manufacturing sites & Tour green tech programs ● Attend climate workforce bootcamps & connect with mentors from green building, clean energy, & industrial trades ● Green Career Fair (green companies + colleges). ● Students are matched with: Paid summer internships & Industry training scholarships ● Companies offer letters of intent to hire talents. / Explain the way your solution works in a few steps (just like sports recruitment)

entries.content: This helps Young Adults and Heavy Industry by: 1. Connecting passion for climate with career paths 2. Rebranding heavy industry as essential and evolving 3. entries.content: We will measure impact by: ● student participants placed into green jobs ● Change in student awareness & perception of green careers (pre/post surveys) ● Industry partners committing to internships or hires ● % of participants from underrepresented backgrounds (women, BIPOC, low-income) / Which stakeholder or stakeholders will you be measuring/testing/understanding - and what will you be measure/testing/understanding to understand if the solution is driving impact?

entries.title: Color was a mobile photo app launched in 2011
entries.content: Color was a mobile photo app launched in 2011 The basic idea was this: when you took a photo, it was geotagged and uploaded to a stream of photos from other people in the same location. Groups of friends were automatically created on the fly depending on who was near you. You could also see all of photos taken in the area even by people you aren’t friends with. / Color raised $41 million pre-launch, and flopped immediately. entries.title: What is the job of a
entries.content: What is the job of a milkshake? / The original idea for Jobs-To-Be-Done came out of marketing research that HBS professor Clay Christensen did with a fast food chain (Book: Competing Against Luck.). The fast food chain wanted to find out how to sell more of its milkshakes. So they interviewed customers that had just bought milkshakes to find out why they had purchased them. (go to next slide) What they found is that a lot of customers bought milkshakes in the morning during their commute to work. (half of milkshakes are bought before 8.30am) They wanted something that would be easy to consume one-handed (while driving), that would take a while to eat (so they would have something to do), and that would keep them full for a while after they got to work. Milkshakes fit the bill perfectly. This surprising discovery led to a whole host of new ideas for how to market and improve on milkshakes.

entries.title: "Your customers are not buying
entries.content: "Your customers are not buying your products, they are hiring them to get a job done." CLAY CHRISTENSEN / Clay Christensen is an expert and leader in a popular framework used by entrepreneurs and product teams to better understand their customers. This is called jobs-to-be-done. / What Jobs-To-Be-Done says is that when a customer buys a product, they’re actually “hiring” that product to do a job for them. There’s some kind of challenge in their life, and they need to hire something to get rid of it. / When we conduct a customer interviews or surveys, we we want to understand the “job” that the product we’re building will do for a customer.

entries.title: "Your customers are not buying
entries.content: "Your customers are not buying your products, they are hiring them to get a job done." CLAY CHRISTENSEN / Clay Christensen is an expert and leader in a popular framework used by entrepreneurs and product teams to better understand their customers. This is called jobs-to-be-done. / What Jobs-To-Be-Done says is that when a customer buys a product, they’re actually “hiring” that product to do a job for them. There’s some kind of challenge in their life, and they need to hire something to get rid of it. / When we conduct a customer interviews or surveys, we we want to understand the “job” that the product we’re building will do for a customer.

entries.content: HOW WE ACHIEVE IT / VOLUNTEERING WITH FRIENDS FOR REWARDS

entries.title: VOLUNTEERING
entries.content: VOLUNTEERING ACTUALLY Builds community Helps teens make new friends Boosts social skills / There are a lot of benefits to volunteering. It helps build community by creating connections between the volunteer and the person they are helping. It is also extremely social, with teens having the opportunity to hang out with a bunch of people who are united towards one cause. It also boosts skills, as it teaches teens initiative, responsibility, and how to effectively communicate with others.

entries.content: BUT NOT ENOUGH PEOPLE VOLUNTEER LONG ENOUGH TO EXPERIENCE THE BENEFITS!#!! / So then, what’s wrong with volunteering? Well, the problem isn’t volunteering itself. It’s that teens don’t volunteer for long enough to realize these benefits, and some don’t even volunteer at all.

entries.title: CO-CREATED BEST PRACTICES
entries.content: CO-CREATED BEST PRACTICES / The Cone of Predictability An important part of knowledge, is to recognize there are things, you do not know. / Co-Created has developed the model below, to illustrate how foresight, predictions and knowledge can be out of our reach, as well as remain in a constant ux. What we don’t know today, we might know tomorrow. / The model states the further we attempt to look into the future, the more unpredictable the assumptions become. / The immediate future might be predictable, but as soon as we move just a little further into the future, assumptions become uncertain, and when we look far into the future, almost everything becomes unpredictable. / But as we attempt to predict the future, we also move into it. / What that means, is that it is important to understand and remember that what used to be unpredictable or uncertain, might not be so today. We need to constantly revise what we know and keep our truths and assumptions up to date. / fl
